items.stem: Under the IB DP Geography IA assessment criteria, how many marks are available for criterion D (written analysis)?
items.markingKey: 9. The IA is marked out of 30 in total.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A significant result proves the hypothesis is true." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It means the null hypothesis can be rejected at a confidence level; there remains a chance of error and other explanations.
items.markingKey: It means the null hypothesis can be rejected at a confidence level; there remains a chance of error and other explanations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between analysis of results and description of results.
items.answer: Description states what the data show (patterns, trends, values); analysis explains why, using geographical theory, statistical tests and links to the fieldwork question.
items.markingKey: Description states what the data show (patterns, trends, values); analysis explains why, using geographical theory, statistical tests and links to the fieldwork question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which an IA on CBD-frame land use in Lisbon shows written analysis.
items.answer: A student mapped land use at 60 points along transects, used chi-squared to test differences by zone and explained anomalies near metro stations. Statistical testing and theory were linked to the question.
items.markingKey: Context (A student mapped land use at 60 points along transects, used chi-squared to test differences by zone and explained anomalies near metro stations.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Statistical testing and theory were linked to the question. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to written analysis.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Fieldwork data: distance from CBD (m) and pedestrian count per 10 min at 8 sites - 100: 210; 300: 160; 500: 145; 700: 90; 900: 110; 1,100: 60; 1,300: 40; 1,500: 30.

Ranking both variables from highest (1) to lowest, calculate Σd² and Spearman's rank (rs = 1 − 6Σd²/(n³ − n)).
items.answer: Distance ranks 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; count ranks 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6, 7, 8; Σd² = 49 + 25 + 9 + 0 + 0 + 9 + 25 + 49 = 166; rs = 1 − (6 × 166)/504 = -0.976 - a strong negative correlation, significant at 0.05 (critical value 0.643 for n = 8).
items.markingKey: Distance ranks 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; count ranks 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6, 7, 8; Σd² = 49 + 25 + 9 + 0 + 0 + 9 + 25 + 49 = 166; rs = 1 − (6 × 166)/504 = -0.976 - a strong negative correlation, significant at 0.05 (critical value 0.643 for n = 8). Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Suggest two ways of presenting river channel data in an IA.
items.answer: Cross-sectional profiles drawn to scale; scatter graphs of width vs velocity with best-fit line; proportional symbols on a map; kite diagrams.
items.markingKey: Cross-sectional profiles drawn to scale; scatter graphs of width vs velocity with best-fit line; proportional symbols on a map; kite diagrams.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Fieldwork data: land use at 60 points in two zones - Zone A: commercial 22, residential 8; Zone B: commercial 9, residential 21.

(a) Calculate the percentage of commercial land use in each zone. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest a statistical test to check whether the difference is significant. [6]
items.answer: (a) A: 22/30 = 73.3%; B: 9/30 = 30.0% (b) Chi-squared test of association using a 2 × 2 contingency table (df = 1, critical value 3.84 at 0.05).
items.markingKey: (a) A: 22/30 = 73.3%; B: 9/30 = 30.0% (b) Chi-squared test of association using a 2 × 2 contingency table (df = 1, critical value 3.84 at 0.05). Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: Explain how a student can produce a high-quality written analysis in a geography IA.
items.answer: Indicative content: Criterion D; linking to the question; appropriate graphs and maps; statistical tests and significance; geographical theory; anomalies; triangulation; example investigation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Criterion D; linking to the question; appropriate graphs and maps; statistical tests and significance; geographical theory; anomalies; triangulation; example investigation. Paper 1 extended-response markbands [10]: 9-10 responds to all demands of the question; accurate, detailed knowledge and understanding; well-developed, relevant examples and case studies with specific (named, located, quantified) detail; balanced, well-structured evaluation leading to a substantiated conclusion. 7-8 responds to most demands; mostly accurate knowledge; examples relevant but not always fully developed; evaluation present but uneven. 5-6 some demands addressed; knowledge partly accurate; examples general or loosely linked; evaluation mostly implicit. 3-4 limited, largely descriptive; little use of examples. 1-2 little relevant knowledge or understanding. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "anomaly".
items.answer: A result that does not fit the general pattern or trend, which should be identified and explained
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a result that does not fit the general pattern or trend, which should be identified and explained. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why statistical significance testing strengthens fieldwork analysis.
items.answer: It shows whether a pattern is likely to be real rather than due to chance, allowing a more confident conclusion about the hypothesis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows whether a pattern is likely to be real rather than due to chance, allowing a more confident conclusion about the hypothesis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why anomalies should be discussed in an IA analysis.
items.answer: They may reveal measurement errors, local factors not included in the hypothesis, or limitations of the method; explaining them shows critical understanding and supports evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They may reveal measurement errors, local factors not included in the hypothesis, or limitations of the method; explaining them shows critical understanding and supports evaluation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student mapped 40 primary schools in a county in Ireland within a study area of 9 km². The mean distance between each point and its nearest neighbour was 0.43 km. Calculate the nearest-neighbour index (Rn = 2d̄√(n/A)) and describe the pattern.
items.answer: Rn = 2 × 0.43 × √(40/9) = 1.81; pattern regular (uniform) (0 = clustered, 1.0 = random, 2.15 = perfectly regular).
items.markingKey: M1 substitution; A1 Rn = 1.81; R1 interpretation: regular (uniform).

items.stem: The following household water use (litres per person per day) from a questionnaire in Cape Town were recorded: 234, 78, 43, 103, 86, 107, 86, 65, 61, 104, 192. Calculate the median, the interquartile range (quartiles as medians of the lower and upper halves) and the standard deviation (σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/n)).
items.markingKey: A1 median 86; M1 quartiles from ordered data (Q1 65, Q3 107); A1 IQR 42; M1 A1 σ = 54.81.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded land-use categories recorded at 60 random sample points in a district of Johannesburg: residential 6, commercial 15, industrial 32, open space 7. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 15 per category; χ² = 28.93; df = 3; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 60/4 = 15; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 28.93; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: reject H₀.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that statistical tests are essential for a high-quality IA analysis?
items.answer: Tests strengthen analysis when appropriate, but must be supported by geographical explanation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: test significance of patterns; quantitative rigour. Against / limitations: small samples limit tests; qualitative analysis and theory are also valued. A supported conclusion might be: Tests strengthen analysis when appropriate, but must be supported by geographical explanation. items.stem: Which of these is the strongest evaluation point?
items.answer: Pedestrian counts were taken only on one Tuesday morning, so they may not represent weekend or evening patterns; repeating at different times would improve reliability.
items.markingKey: Pedestrian counts were taken only on one Tuesday morning, so they may not represent weekend or evening patterns; repeating at different times would improve reliability.. Evaluation should be specific, linked to results and suggest improvements.

items.stem: A student claims: "A longer IA scores more marks." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only the first 2,500 words are assessed; concise, focused writing scores best.
items.markingKey: Only the first 2,500 words are assessed; concise, focused writing scores best. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between validity and reliability.
items.answer: Reliability is whether a method gives consistent results when repeated; validity is whether it measures what it is intended to measure and answers the question.
items.markingKey: Reliability is whether a method gives consistent results when repeated; validity is whether it measures what it is intended to measure and answers the question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using an IA on perception of tourism in Dubrovnik as an example, explain validity of questionnaire data.
items.answer: A questionnaire of 50 residents showed most opposed cruise tourism. Sample composition and question wording affected validity.
items.markingKey: Context (A questionnaire of 50 residents showed most opposed cruise tourism.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sample composition and question wording affected validity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to validity of questionnaire data.

items.stem: Households in a ward in Bristol by tenure: owner-occupied 698, privately rented 602, social housing 246. A student will interview 100 households using stratified sampling. Calculate how many of each tenure type should be interviewed, and give one advantage of stratified sampling here.
items.answer: owner-occupied 45.1 ≈ 45; privately rented 38.9 ≈ 39; social housing 15.9 ≈ 16; advantage: each tenure group is represented in proportion, reducing sampling bias.
items.markingKey: M1 (group ÷ total) × sample; A1 all three values (rounded, total = sample size); R1 advantage.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: IA criteria (DP Geography) - A fieldwork question and context 3; B method(s) 3; C quality and treatment of information 6; D written analysis 9; E conclusion 2; F evaluation 3; G formal requirements 4.

(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest why criterion D carries the most marks. [6]
items.answer: (a) Total 30; C + D = 15 = 50% (b) Analysis shows the student's ability to interpret data using geographic understanding, the main skill the IA assesses.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "word limit"?
options: The maximum of 2,500 words for the geography IA, excluding labels, tables, references and appendices
The IA criterion (9 marks) rewarding analysis of results linked to the fieldwork question, using evidence, geographic theory and anomalies
The 1-hour HL exam on the HL core extension, with three questions of which one is answered; each has part (a) for 12 marks and part (b) for 16 marks
The probability that a result could have occurred by chance; geographers usually accept results at the 0.05 (95%) level
items.answer: The maximum of 2,500 words for the geography IA, excluding labels, tables, references and appendices
items.markingKey: A. "word limit" is the maximum of 2,500 words for the geography IA, excluding labels, tables, references and appendices.

items.stem: Briefly explain why evaluation should consider the effect of weaknesses on the results.
items.answer: Simply listing problems is not enough; explaining how a limitation (e.g. small sample, timing, equipment) may have biased or limited the results shows understanding of reliability and validity.

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Fieldwork record: temperature readings at a site repeated 5 times - 18.2, 18.6, 18.4, 21.9, 18.3 °C.

Identify the likely error and calculate the mean with and without it.

items.answer: Indicative content: Criteria E and F; answering the question; reliability and validity; specific weaknesses and their effects; improvements; formal requirements (G); word limit.

items.stem: Paper 3 (HL) lasts:
items.answer: 1 hour
items.markingKey: A. It is worth 28 marks and 20% of the HL grade.

items.answer: Higher bands require balance, different perspectives and a justified conclusion.
items.markingKey: Higher bands require balance, different perspectives and a justified conclusion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why using specific case studies at different scales is valuable.
items.answer: Detailed, place-specific evidence at local, national and global scales supports arguments, shows how processes vary, and is rewarded in the markbands. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Detailed, place-specific evidence at local, national and global scales supports arguments, shows how processes vary, and is rewarded in the markbands. items.stem: Briefly describe the rise of China as a global power and explain what it reveals about synthesis of power and global interactions.
items.answer: China combines the largest economy by PPP, the Belt and Road Initiative and growing technology firms. Economic, political and cultural power interact at different scales.
items.markingKey: Context (China combines the largest economy by PPP, the Belt and Road Initiative and growing technology firms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Economic, political and cultural power interact at different scales. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to synthesis of power and global interactions.

items.stem: The merchandise exports of an East African country was 66.1 US$ billion in 1990 and 53.0 US$ billion in 2010. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (53.0 − 66.1) ÷ 66.1 × 100; A1 -19.8% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Graph description: share of world GDP (PPP) held by the G7 fell from about 50% in 1990 to about 30% in 2023, while BRICS (original five) rose from about 16% to about 32%.

(a) Calculate the change in percentage points for each group. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, use the data to discuss a shift in global power. [6]
items.answer: (a) G7: −20; BRICS: +16 (b) Economic power has moved towards emerging economies, with BRICS now larger than the G7 at PPP, supporting the idea of a multipolar world, though G7 countries still lead in finance, military and technology.
items.markingKey: (a) G7: −20; BRICS: +16 (b) Economic power has moved towards emerging economies, with BRICS now larger than the G7 at PPP, supporting the idea of a multipolar world, though G7 countries still lead in finance, military and technology. items.answer: States remain most powerful, but non-state actors increasingly shape global interactions.

items.stem: Distinguish between Paper 3 part (a) and Paper 3 part (b).
items.answer: Part (a) (12 marks) usually asks students to explain or analyse a process or pattern; part (b) (16 marks) requires discussion or evaluation with perspectives, synthesis and a conclusion.

items.stem: Explain why synthesis across the HL themes strengthens a Paper 3 essay.
items.answer: Linking global interactions, development, culture and risk shows understanding of interconnections and allows a more nuanced, evaluative argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Linking global interactions, development, culture and risk shows understanding of interconnections and allows a more nuanced, evaluative argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Plan a 16-mark answer to: "To what extent is global power still concentrated in a few countries?"
items.answer: Introduction defining power and key concepts; arguments for concentration (USA/China military, IMF voting, TNC headquarters); arguments against (BRICS expansion, G20, non-state actors, civil society, social media); perspectives (emerging economies, NGOs); scales; conclusion: power remains concentrated but is becoming more multipolar and diffuse.

items.stem: Approximate data for Mexico: life expectancy 74.8 years; expected years of schooling 14.9; mean years of schooling 9.2; GNI per capita US$19,100 (PPP). Using the UNDP method - life expectancy index = (LE − 20)/65; education index = (MYS/15 + EYS/18)/2, with EYS capped at 18; income index = (ln GNI − ln 100)/(ln 75,000 − ln 100); HDI = geometric mean of the three indices - calculate the HDI and its category.
items.markingKey: A1 LEI 0.843; A1 EI 0.721; A1 II 0.793; M1 geometric mean; A1 HDI 0.784, high.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Non-state actors are now more powerful than states in shaping global interactions."

items.stem: Which statistical test is most suitable for testing whether observed frequencies differ from expected frequencies across categories?
items.answer: Chi-squared test

A: 33.6, 8.2; B: 22.8, 5.1; C: 32.8, 8.1; D: 42.9, 11.0; E: 62.9, 16.7; F: 8.6, 1.5; G: 31.3, 8.9; H: 22.7, 6.4.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 8: 0.643).
items.answer: Σd² = 8; rs = 1 − 6×8/(8³ − 8) = 0.905; a positive correlation that is significant at the 0.05 level.

items.stem: "Global interactions bring more benefits than risks." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of different stakeholders.
items.answer: Benefits are large but unevenly shared; risks can be reduced with resilience and fair governance.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (b) indicative content - for: trade and FDI reduce poverty (China, Vietnam); cultural exchange and technology. Against: financial contagion, supply-chain shocks, environmental damage; unequal power and loss of identity. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "written analysis (criterion D)"?
options: The four key concepts of the course - place, process, power and possibility - plus scale, spatial interactions and sustainability
The IA criterion (9 marks) rewarding analysis of results linked to the fieldwork question, using evidence, geographic theory and anomalies
A statement that there is no relationship or difference, which statistical tests try to reject
The IA criterion (2 marks) for a clear, consistent answer to the fieldwork question based on the analysis
items.answer: The IA criterion (9 marks) rewarding analysis of results linked to the fieldwork question, using evidence, geographic theory and anomalies
items.markingKey: B. "written analysis (criterion D)" is the IA criterion (9 marks) rewarding analysis of results linked to the fieldwork question, using evidence, geographic theory and anomalies.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "geographic concepts".
items.answer: The four key concepts of the course - place, process, power and possibility - plus scale, spatial interactions and sustainability

items.stem: Which criterion assesses the fieldwork question and geographic context?
items.answer: Criterion A (3 marks)
items.markingKey: B. A requires a focused question, context and a map.

items.stem: Explain the difference between description of results and analysis of results.
items.answer: Description states what the data show (patterns, trends, values); analysis explains why, using geographical theory, statistical tests and links to the fieldwork question.
items.markingKey: Description states what the data show (patterns, trends, values); analysis explains why, using geographical theory, statistical tests and links to the fieldwork question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A Paper 3 essay should present only one side of the argument." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Higher bands require balance, different perspectives and a justified conclusion.
items.markingKey: Higher bands require balance, different perspectives and a justified conclusion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why sampling strategy affects the validity of fieldwork results.
items.answer: Random, systematic and stratified sampling reduce bias and ensure representativeness; opportunistic or poorly distributed samples may give misleading results.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Random, systematic and stratified sampling reduce bias and ensure representativeness; opportunistic or poorly distributed samples may give misleading results. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Analysis is just describing graphs." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Analysis must interpret patterns, explain them with geographic concepts, use evidence and consider anomalies.
items.markingKey: Analysis must interpret patterns, explain them with geographic concepts, use evidence and consider anomalies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a descriptive essay and an evaluative essay.
items.answer: A descriptive essay lists information about a topic; an evaluative essay weighs evidence and arguments to reach a justified judgement.
items.markingKey: A descriptive essay lists information about a topic; an evaluative essay weighs evidence and arguments to reach a justified judgement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The evaluation should only list things that went wrong." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It should assess strengths and weaknesses, their effect on results and specific improvements.
items.markingKey: It should assess strengths and weaknesses, their effect on results and specific improvements. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Suggest how a student can stay within the 2,500-word limit.
items.answer: Use tables, labelled graphs and annotated maps (which are not counted), avoid repetition, keep the introduction and methods concise, and focus analysis on the question.
items.markingKey: Use tables, labelled graphs and annotated maps (which are not counted), avoid repetition, keep the introduction and methods concise, and focus analysis on the question.

items.stem: A student mapped 58 convenience stores in a district of Tokyo within a study area of 16 km². The mean distance between each point and its nearest neighbour was 0.17 km. Calculate the nearest-neighbour index (Rn = 2d̄√(n/A)) and describe the pattern.
items.answer: Rn = 2 × 0.17 × √(58/16) = 0.65; pattern clustered (0 = clustered, 1.0 = random, 2.15 = perfectly regular).
items.markingKey: M1 substitution; A1 Rn = 0.65; R1 interpretation: clustered.

items.stem: Approximate globalisation sub-index scores (0-100): Bolivia - economic 58, social 59, political 74; Chad - economic 29, social 25, political 67. Assuming the three dimensions are weighted equally (as in the KOF index), calculate the overall index for each country. Explain one limitation of composite globalisation indices.
items.answer: Bolivia: 63.7; Chad: 40.3; limitation: weights are arbitrary, national averages hide regional differences, and data on informal or illicit flows are missing.
items.markingKey: A1 63.7; A1 40.3. R1 limitation.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the land cover at 100 points sampled across a drainage basin in Devon: forest 2, grassland 49, arable 17, urban 32. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 25 per category; χ² = 48.72; df = 3; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 100/4 = 25; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 48.72; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: reject H₀.
